title: Food Webs and Interactions in Ecosystems
seo_title: Grade 6 Science: Food Webs and Interactions in Ecosystems Worksheets (MATATAG)
standard_text: Living things interact with each other (predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism, parasitism) and with abiotic factors; food webs show feeding relationships in an ecosystem. (summary of the MATATAG Science curriculum, Grade 6, Quarter 2: Living Things)
meta_desc: Free Grade 6 Science worksheets (MATATAG, Quarter 2: Living Things): biotic and abiotic factors, relationships between species, energy flow and cycles, food webs and change in ecosystems. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Energy flows through food webs; matter cycles; populations are limited by resources.
body_html:
How to think about it

An ecosystem is the living (biotic) and non-living (abiotic) parts of an area and how they interact.

  • Symbiosis: mutualism (both benefit), commensalism (one benefits) and parasitism (one is harmed).
  • Only about 10% of the energy at one level passes to the next, so food chains are short.
  • Food, water, space and predators limit populations; succession slowly changes an ecosystem over time.
Example

A tick feeds on a carabao. What relationship is this?

the tick benefits

the carabao is harmed

Answer: parasitism

Example

Is sunlight biotic or abiotic?

it is not living

Answer: abiotic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking energy is recycled like matter (it flows one way).
  • Mixing up commensalism and mutualism.
  • Thinking populations can grow forever.

faq.q: What is the difference between biotic and abiotic factors?
faq.a: Biotic factors are living things. Abiotic factors are non-living, like sunlight, water and temperature.

faq.q: Why are there fewer top predators than producers?
faq.a: Energy is lost at each level, so there is less energy available for animals at the top.
The slow change in the plants and animals of an ecosystem over time, such as a burned forest growing back.

items.q: Mark observes that a mosquito feeds on a person's blood. What kind of interaction is this?
items.e: In parasitism, one benefits and the other is harmed.

items.q: Fish in a pond die when the water becomes too acidic. Which physical factor is most important here?
items.e: Physical factors in the environment affect which organisms can survive.

items.q: What is an ecosystem?
c: only the animals in a forest
all the living things in an area and the non-living things they interact with
items.e: Biotic and abiotic parts interact.

items.q: Why is only about 10% of energy passed on to the next level of a food chain?
c: Most energy is used for life processes or lost as heat.
items.e: This is shown in an energy pyramid.

items.q: Jasmine observes that bacteria in your intestines get food and help you digest. What kind of interaction is this?

items.q: Which organisms recycle nutrients from dead matter back into the soil?

items.q: What is symbiosis?
c: a close relationship between two different species
items.e: It can be mutualism, commensalism or parasitism.

items.q: What is the role of producers in an ecosystem?
c: They capture the Sun's energy and make food by photosynthesis.
items.e: Producers are at the base.

cattle egrets eat insects stirred up by grazing cows

items.e: Energy is lost at each step, so the last organism in the chain gets the least.

items.q: In Hazel's food web, what does an arrow from one organism to another show?

the direction energy and matter move when one is eaten
items.e: Arrows point from the food to the eater.

items.q: Vincent's energy pyramid shows 2,000 units of energy in the producers. About 10% passes to each level above. About how much energy reaches the tertiary consumers?
items.e: Divide by 10 for each level: 2,000 → 200 → 20 → 2.

items.q: Look at the pond food web. Which of these is food for the frog?
items.e: The arrow goes from the snail to the frog, so the frog eats a snail.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. Most of the small fish are removed. Which population is most likely to increase at first?
items.e: Only the small fish eats zooplankton in this web, so fewer of them are eaten.

items.q: This is a school garden food web. Which animal eats the grasshopper?
items.e: An arrow goes from the grasshopper to the spider.

items.q: Use the pond food web. In this web, the heron's food is: frog, small fish. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only animals.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. What does the small fish eat?
items.e: The arrow goes from the zooplankton to the small fish, so the small fish eats zooplankton.

items.q: Use the pond food web. In this web, the snail's food is: algae, water lettuce. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only plants (producers).

items.q: This is a forest food web. In this web, the Philippine deer's food is: narra tree, berry bush. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only plants (producers).

items.q: Use the pond food web. How many kinds of food does the mosquito larva eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the mosquito larva: algae.

items.q: This is a pond food web. Which animal eats the frog?
items.e: An arrow goes from the frog to the heron.

items.q: Use the pond food web. How many kinds of food does the frog eat in this web?
items.e: Count the arrows pointing to the frog: dragonfly, snail.

items.q: What is a food web?
c: many food chains that are linked together
items.e: Most animals eat more than one thing.

items.q: Look at the coral reef food web. What does the parrotfish eat?
items.e: The arrow goes from the seaweed to the parrotfish, so the parrotfish eats seaweed.

items.q: This is a coral reef food web. What does the green turtle eat?
items.e: The arrow goes from the seaweed to the green turtle, so the green turtle eats seaweed.

items.q: This is a meadow food web. Which animal eats the wildflowers?
items.e: An arrow goes from the wildflowers to the rabbit.

items.q: Look at the pond food web. What does the dragonfly eat?
items.e: The arrow goes from the mosquito larva to the dragonfly, so the dragonfly eats a mosquito larva.

items.q: Pond food web: algae and duckweed are eaten by tadpoles and snails. Fish eat tadpoles. Herons eat fish and frogs. Which living things are producers?
items.e: Producers are the plants and algae.

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the small fish eats zooplankton. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Lake food chain: algae → zooplankton → minnow → walleye → osprey. What eats the walleye?
items.e: The arrow from walleye points to the osprey.

items.q: Look at the meadow food web. In this web, the rabbit's food is: grass, wildflowers. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: It eats only plants (producers).

items.q: Look at the food web of a coral reef. In this web, the zooplankton eats phytoplankton. What kind of consumer is it?
items.e: Herbivores eat only plants, carnivores only animals, omnivores both.

items.q: Two species of barnacles live on the same rock. When one is removed, the other spreads into its area. What does this show?
items.e: Removing a competitor frees resources.

items.q: Ana's graph shows native fish in a lake area. An invasive fish arrived in 2016. Which claim does the data support?
c: The graph shows the arrival caused growth.
The native fish population grew after an invasive fish arrived.
The native fish population declined after an invasive fish arrived.
items.e: The numbers drop after 2016.

items.q: Patricia reads: “A disease kills many bats.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: By how much did native fish decrease from 2015 to 2019 in Camille's data?
Andrea reads: “Hunters remove most of the sea otters from a coast.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Arnel studies a burned forest recovering over many years. Which stage comes after “grasses and wildflowers”?
items.e: This gradual recovery is called succession.

items.q: Mae reads: “Kudzu vines spread over forests in the South.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?

items.q: Nico reads: “A volcano covers land with ash.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?

items.q: Liza's graph shows frogs in a lake area. A fungus disease arrived in 2016. Which claim does the data support?

items.q: Diane watches an abandoned farm field over 50 years. What process is changing the field from grasses to forest?
items.e: Communities change over time after a disturbance.

items.q: A bird nests in a tree and the tree is not affected. What kind of relationship is this?
items.e: One benefits; the other is not helped or harmed.

items.q: Rose reads: “A long drought dries up streams.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Rodel graphs barn owls and mice on a farm. When mice increase, owls increase a year later. Why?
c: More food (mice) supports more owl chicks.
items.e: Predators follow prey.

items.q: Lance studies a burned forest recovering over many years. Which stage comes after “bare soil or rock”?
items.e: This gradual recovery is called succession.

items.q: Jericho reads: “Wolves are returned to a national park.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Arnel studies a burned forest recovering over many years. Which stage comes after “shrubs and small trees”?
items.e: This gradual recovery is called succession.

items.q: Diane finds that cowbirds lay eggs in other birds' nests, and the other birds raise the cowbird chicks. What kind of relationship is this?

items.q: Kristine reads: “A flood covers a river valley with mud.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
